Longlisted for the Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction Shortlisted for the British Academy Book Prize for Global Cultural Understanding Longlisted for the Cundill History Prize A New York Times Notable Book A ri veting, masterfully researched account of the bold innovators who adapted the Chinese language to the modern world, transforming China into a superpower in the process What does it take to reinvent the world's oldest living language? China today is one of the world's most powerful nations, yet just a century ago it was a crumbling empire with literacy reserved for the elite few, left behind in the wake of Western technology. In Kingdom of Characters, Jing Tsu shows that China's most daunting challenge was a linguistic one: to make the formidable Chinese language - a 2,200-year-old writing system that was daunting to natives and foreigners alike - accessible to a globalized, digital world. Kingdom of Characters follows the bold innovators who adapted the Chinese script - and the value-system it represents - to the technological advances that would shape the twentieth century and beyond, from the telegram to the typewriter to the smartphone. From the exiled reformer who risked death to advocate for Mandarin as a national language to the imprisoned computer engineer who devised input codes for Chinese characters on the lid of a teacup, generations of scholars, missionaries, librarians, politicians, inventors, nationalists and revolutionaries alike understood the urgency of their task and its world-shaping consequences. With larger-than-life characters and a thrilling narrative, Kingdom of Characters offers an astonishingly original perspective on one of the twentieth century's most dramatic transformations.

### Review

...

Writing about writing is hard; writing about Chinese writing in English is devilish. Strokes, logographs, ideographs - even the basic terminology can cloud the mind like a calligraphy brush loaded with too much ink. Jing Tsu's brilliant solution is to focus on characters - not the ones written from left to right, top to bottom, but the actual living, breathing, thinking individuals who, since the start of the twentieth century, did everything they could to adapt the Chinese language and writing system to the modern world. In Kingdom of Characters, Tsu introduces us to a cast of unforgettable figures: the wanted fugitive who pushes for Mandarin as China's national tongue; the engineer and bamboo expert who develops a Chinese typewriter; the railway administrator who tries to figure out how to send telegrams in a language without an alphabet. Along the way, Tsu tells an essential story of modern China: a country at once transformed and yet deeply traditional -- Peter Hessler

##### All you would have asked about Chinese characters

Reviewed in the United Kingdom on 3 January 2024

...

If we are non-specialists, we very probably like Chinese characters, doubtless mainly for their elegance, while being secretly grateful to have inherited a simpler system; but while imagining a Confucian sage wielding his brush, in all probability, we give little thought to the practical implications of adapting a 3000-year-old script to the modern world.

Jing Tzu treats us to a kind of picaresque novel, in which her hero — Chinese script — emerges victorious from a series of adventures, covering the period of its contact with the “West” (essentially America).

Its first adventure was to survive in an approximation of its traditional form.

Next, it needed to acquire that essential of modern commerce, a typewriter — reasonably simple if you’ve 44 keys arranged in a conventional order in four neat rows, but altogether more daunting when the theoretical number of characters is limitless, but even an everyday selectiom amounts to thousands.

The arrival of (mainly foreign-owned) railways brought in its wake the telegraph — but how do you squidge a Chinese character down a wire? Insofar as I’d given any thought to the matter, I’d assumed messages were sent in alphabetic guise. Not so! There wasn’t a reliable way of transcribing Chinese, nor a single agreed pronunciation for a given character; and as characters are units of meaning, not sound, often the identical syllable can be represented by several, sometimes many characters, giving greater clarity in writing than speech. The solution was to use morse code, like all telegraphy at the time — however, not the letters used for European languages, but by ascribing a numerical value to each character, which worked, but was expensive because it increased transmission time.

The Chinese have long had a (cumbersome) system for looking up words in a dictionary; there are a small(-ish 214) number of elements one of which occurs in every character, (misleadingly) called a “radical”; the sections of the dictionary are organised according to radical in ascending number of strokes, after which the characters are listed by number of strokes. However, this system was not adequate for consulting a library catalogue, so in order to make it easier for readers to find their way through a card index, librarians had to find ways of analysing characters into their constituent parts.

Communism brought two important developments; one was an agreed and official way of transcribing Chinese into Latin letters, the “pinyin” that changed Peking to Beijing; the second was the simplification of a certain number of frequently-used characters. Pinyin is used alongside characters, as a reference, but has not replaced them.

Chinese characters are a code, but many steps in their adaptation to modernity have involved representing the code by a code, but never more so than in their latest adventure, which has brought them to computers and mobile phones.

If the image of a Confucian scholar honing his brushwork may be out of date, each of the developments Jing Tzu chronicles was achieved by one or several devoted, often fanatical, scholars, who endured severe privations to complete their task, and as much as a history of technology, “Kingdom of Characters” is an affectionate biography of these heroic pioneers.T

# Jing Tsu

## About the author

Jing Tsu, a Guggenheim Fellow, is a cultural historian of modern China at Yale. An expert on language, literature, history, culture, and science and technology from the 19th century to now, she is John M. Schiff Professor of East Asian Languages and Literatures & Comparative Literature, a member of the Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs, and a senior fellow at the MacMillan Center for International & Area Studies. She has written for The New York Times, The New York Times Book Review, and Financial Times. She was the cultural commentator for NBC at the 2022 Beijing Olympics. Her authored/edited books include: Failure, Nationalism, and Literature; Sound and Script in Chinese Diaspora; Science and Technology in Modern China, 1880s-1940s; Global Chinese Literature. Her most recent non-fiction book, Kingdom of Characters: The Language Revolution That Made China Modern (Riverhead, 2022), has received wide international acclaim in The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, The New Yorker, The Economist, Wired, Science, Nature, Physics World, The Times, The Spectator, The Telegraph, The Guardian, The Scotsman, Times Literary Supplement, London Review of Books, South China Morning Post (Hong Kong), NRC (The Netherlands), Frankfurter Allgemeine (Germany), etc. The subject of more than 30 podcasts and webinars, Kingdom of Characters was nominated for several international book prizes across multiple categories, including the Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction, the Cundhill History Prize, and the British Academy Book Prize for Global Cultural Understanding. Her book was named a "Notable Books of 2022" by The New York Times and a "Best Non-Fiction of 2022" by The Washington Post.
